newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: FEATURE - EU presidency Luxembourg worries about own jobless.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - EU presidency Luxembourg worries about own jobless.

text.p: Wealthy Luxembourg boasts the lowest jobless rate in the European Union where unemployment has become the scourge of the decade, but even the Grand Duchy is rattled by a steadily rising trend in its figures.

Luxembourg, which took over the rotating EU presidency in July, is so concerned about the plight of Europe's 18 million unemployed it has put jobs at the top of its six-month EU agenda and will host a special summit on employment in November.

"For this country, an unemployment rate of (around) 3.5 percent is unexpectedly high given the macro-economic background and because we are net creators of jobs," Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker said last month.

At the same time, in tackling the particular problems of a labour market where more than half those in employment commute from abroad or are resident foreigners, Luxembourg has taken initiatives which it says might also work in other EU states.

European Union figures put unemployment in the Grand Duchy at 3.7 percent in both April and May -- the highest level since 4.0 percent in December 1995 -- and a rise from 3.4 percent in January this year. For most of 1996 the rate stood between 2.9 and 3.2 percent.
However it still has the lowest level in the 15-nation EU where average unemployment for May was 10.8 percent.

Luxembourg, which enjoys low inflation and healthy growth, has seen its financial services and communications sectors flourish in particular, helping to offset the 20-year decline of its steel industry. Tourism is also a big employer.

But most new openings are snapped up by skilled workers from neighbouring regions in Germany, France and Belgium who face high unemployment at home and are attracted by the relatively good salaries on offer in the Grand Duchy.
At the same time, their more generous unemployment benefits make Luxembourgers less willing to accept low paid jobs.
"Problem areas we have are basic education, adaption to demand and vocational training," Jean Zahlen, a senior advisor at the Luxembourg employment ministry, told Reuters.
Basic education could be better focused on market needs, he said, while a law was being finalised to give financial incentives to firms which give vocational training to the unemployed.
"Our best results come from focused vocational training with very small groups," he added.
SEEKING SUCCESSFUL IDEAS FOR NOVEMBER SUMMIT
Preparing to host the EU summit in November which will look at ways to create jobs and cut unemployment, Juncker has asked each member state to submit successful ideas for getting people into work.

Examples from Luxembourg, which has a resident population of only 418,000, could include youth employment schemes as well as the focused vocational training and tax benefits for firms taking on the jobless, Zahlen said.
One Luxembourg youth scheme that offered 18 months' work in public services with training on a minimum wage led to 80 percent of participants finding a job outside the scheme.
A private sector scheme where the state contributed 50 percent to a minimum wage resulted in 75 percent finding jobs.
The government has also given Luxembourg's public employment service a more active role than before, with a number of staff with experience of the private sector being taken on.
But focusing on "employability" has been seen by wary trade unions as meaning simply flexibility for the employer.
Discussions on flexibility between unions and employers are currently blocked, with unions first demanding a reduction in working time from 40 hours a week.
OECD CRITICISMS

In its April annual economic survey on Luxembourg the Paris-based OECD think-tank was critical of the country's rigid wage formation system, strict employment protection rules, and generous welfare system.

It recommended that wage indexation be phased out, the minimum wage lowered, and early retirement and disability schemes limited. Taxes and social security contributions at the bottom end of the wage scale might also be further reduced, it said.
But Luxembourg rejected the criticism, and Juncker insists that flexibility must not mean deregulation. Workers who have jobs must not be made to feel they are at risk, he says.
Robert Goebbels, the economics minister, says meanwhile that "as long as inflation is lower than our direct competitors we don't have a problem with wage indexation."

One Luxembourg economist, who declined to be named, said it was politically very difficult to touch salary indexation, social benefits and minimum wages while Luxembourg continued to flourish economically compared to its neigbours.

"You can't have economic growth systematically above three percent even when the others are going through economic crises and say we are going to reduce all your established social benefits because they are much too expensive.
"They are trying to do it but its a very gradual, long process," he said.
Things could change though if Luxembourg were to see another crisis, such as experienced during the steel decline, he added.
"Then Luxembourg...made efforts to diminish salary costs and avoid a big catastrophe. They completely renovated their industrial tissue, accepting wage cuts and training," he said.
"In lean times they have shown their willingness, in fat times measures are much more difficult to get through.
